title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: sqrt()

sqrt(64)
#| [1] 8
64 |> sqrt()
#| [1] 8


traditional use of functions: function(argument)
piping: argument |> function()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: sqrt()

sqrt(64)
#| [1] 8
64 |> sqrt()
#| [1] 8


another way to think about this is that piping reverses the phrasing
in the traditional use of functions, we write the verb and then the noun
with piping, we write the noun and then the verb

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Why would I do this?

I’ll share illustrative examples, highlighting 3 reasons why piping can be useful
I’ll explain the details later
for now, focus on what’s different in the piping examples

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Setup for some coming examples

load some packages:


library(ggplot2) # for ggplot()
library(baseverse) # for base_when()


import the NHANES data:


nhanes <- read.csv('nhanes_l.csv')

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: a ggplot scatterplot

ggplot(data = nhanes, mapping = aes(x = bpxodi1, y = bpxosy1)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = 'Diastolic (mmHg)', y = 'Systolic (mmHg)')

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: a ggplot scatterplot

with piping, I could instead write this:


nhanes |> ggplot(aes(x = bmxht, y = bmxwt)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = 'Diastolic (mmHg)', y = 'Systolic (mmHg)')


notice that this allows me to omit the data argument in ggplot()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: cholesterol

from A Slower Introduction to R:


nhanes$cholesterol <- base_when(
  'Desirable' = (nhanes$lbxtc < 200),
  'Borderline high' = (nhanes$lbxtc >= 200) & (nhanes$lbxtc < 240),
  'High' = (nhanes$lbxtc >= 240)
)

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: cholesterol

with piping, I could instead write this:


nhanes <- nhanes |>
  transform(cholesterol = base_when(
    'Desirable' = (lbxtc < 200),
    'Borderline high' = (lbxtc >= 200) & (lbxtc < 240),
    'High' = (lbxtc >= 240)
  ))


notice that this allows me to omit dollar-sign notation

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Example: a data snippet

suppose that I want to glance at the data for the subset of people with a history of smoking:


head(subset(
  nhanes,
  smoking == 'History of smoking',
  select = c(hypertension, smoking)
))


this is difficult to read because it nests a long use of subset() within head()

title: Session 1: Piping
Session 1: Piping
Session 1: Piping
text:
In summary

you can use piping to avoid the data argument
you can use piping to avoid dollar-sign notation
you can use piping to avoid nested functions

title: Session 1: Piping
section: Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?
text:
Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?

possibly, yes!
piping is a core feature of the tidyverse, in packages like dplyr
originally, the tidyverse used the character sequence %>%

title: Session 1: Piping
section: Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?
text:
Haven’t I seen something like this somewhere else?

in 2021, base R added support for piping, using the character sequence |>
this sequence is known as the native pipe because it is part of base R



With the introduction of the native pipe, many tidyverse users are transitioning to |>, but it’s still possible to use %>% with tidyverse packages.

title: Session 1: Piping
section: So how do I do this?
text:
So how do I do this?

in general, the pattern is: argument |> function()
more precisely, because many functions have multiple possible arguments, the pattern is: first argument of the function |> function()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
mean()

without piping:


mean(nhanes$bpxodi1, na.rm = TRUE)
#| [1] 74.97469


with piping:


nhanes$bpxodi1 |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
#| [1] 74.97469


notice that I’ve kept the na.rm argument in mean()
the phrasing is roughly: “with diastolic blood pressure, take the mean, and ignore missing values when you do so”

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
head()

without piping:


head(nhanes, n = 3)


this shows the first 3 rows of nhanes
with piping:


nhanes |> head(n = 3) 


notice that I’ve kept the n argument in head()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
head() and dim()

without piping:


dim(head(nhanes, n = 3))


with piping:


nhanes |> 
  head(n = 3) |>
  dim()


this forms a longer pipeline
each pipe adds to the result up to that point

title: Session 1: Piping

text:
Exercise 1

Create a script for today’s session.
Include code at the top for importing the NHANES data file. Hint: you might first use RStudio’s built-in import tool, as explained here.
Use piping to round() \(\pi\) to 3 digits. Hint: \(\pi\) is a built-in number in R, stored as pi.
Use piping with nrow() to find the number of rows in the data.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Exercise 1

Use piping with tail() to view the last 3 rows of the data.
Use piping with names() to view all the variable names.
Use piping with names() and head() to view the first few variable names.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Setup for some coming examples

let me first define a mini version of the NHANES data:


minidata <- nhanes[1:8, c('ridageyr', 'asthma', 'smoking', 'bmxht')]



This code uses bracket notation, which I won’t be covering in this workshop series.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Setup for some coming examples

the first few rows of minidata are:


minidata |> head()
#|   ridageyr            asthma            smoking bmxht
#| 1       43                No History of smoking 179.5
#| 2       66                No History of smoking 174.2
#| 3       44                No                 No 152.9
#| 4       43                No                 No    NA
#| 5       65 History of asthma                 No    NA
#| 6       34                No History of smoking 173.3



For the exercises, please continue to use the full NHANES data.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset()

to subset to people with a history of smoking:


subset(minidata, smoking == 'History of smoking')
#|   ridageyr asthma            smoking bmxht
#| 1       43     No History of smoking 179.5
#| 2       66     No History of smoking 174.2
#| 6       34     No History of smoking 173.3
#| 8       27     No History of smoking 168.2

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset() with piping

with piping:


minidata |> subset(smoking == 'History of smoking')
#|   ridageyr asthma            smoking bmxht
#| 1       43     No History of smoking 179.5
#| 2       66     No History of smoking 174.2
#| 6       34     No History of smoking 173.3
#| 8       27     No History of smoking 168.2

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Exercise 2

Use piping to subset the data to individuals with a history of smoking (smoking). Hint: first use table() or unique() to see the unique values of smoking.
Use piping with subset() to subset the data to individuals who are 25 years of age or younger.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Exercise 2

Add code to the top of the script for loading ggplot2.
Use piping with ggplot() to make a scatterplot with diastolic blood pressure (bpxodi1) on the x axis and systolic blood pressure (bpxosy1) on the y axis, subsetting to individuals who are 65 years of age (ridageyr) or older and not missing a measurement of systolic blood pressure. Hint: you can use is.na().

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset()’s select

to select just the asthma and smoking variables:


subset(minidata, select = c(asthma, smoking))
#|              asthma            smoking
#| 1                No History of smoking
#| 2                No History of smoking
#| 3                No                 No
#| 4                No                 No
#| 5 History of asthma                 No
#| 6                No History of smoking
#| 7                No                 No
#| 8                No History of smoking

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset()’s select with piping

with piping:


minidata |> subset(select = c(asthma, smoking))
#|              asthma            smoking
#| 1                No History of smoking
#| 2                No History of smoking
#| 3                No                 No
#| 4                No                 No
#| 5 History of asthma                 No
#| 6                No History of smoking
#| 7                No                 No
#| 8                No History of smoking

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Exercise 3

Use piping with subset() to select just the ridageyr, country, and smoking variables.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset()’s select

to drop the ridageyr variable:


subset(minidata, select = -ridageyr)
#|              asthma            smoking bmxht
#| 1                No History of smoking 179.5
#| 2                No History of smoking 174.2
#| 3                No                 No 152.9
#| 4                No                 No    NA
#| 5 History of asthma                 No    NA
#| 6                No History of smoking 173.3
#| 7                No                 No 155.9
#| 8                No History of smoking 168.2


notice the minus sign

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Dropping variables

subset(minidata, select = -ridageyr)


this simply returns a version of the data without the ridageyr variable
minidata remains untouched
to truly drop a variable, use object assignment to replace minidata:


minidata <- subset(minidata, select = -asthma)

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset()’s select with piping

with piping:


minidata <- minidata |> subset(select = -asthma)


minidata now looks like this:


minidata |> head()
#|   ridageyr            smoking bmxht
#| 1       43 History of smoking 179.5
#| 2       66 History of smoking 174.2
#| 3       44                 No 152.9
#| 4       43                 No    NA
#| 5       65                 No    NA
#| 6       34 History of smoking 173.3

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset()’s select with piping

to drop the ridageyr and smoking variables with piping:


minidata <- minidata |> subset(select = -c(ridageyr, smoking))


notice the minus sign and c()

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
subset()’s select with piping

minidata now looks like this:


minidata |> head()
#|   bmxht
#| 1 179.5
#| 2 174.2
#| 3 152.9
#| 4    NA
#| 5    NA
#| 6 173.3

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Exercise 4

Use piping with subset() to obtain a version of the data without the smoking variable. You do not need to replace the original data.
Use piping with subset() to obtain a version of the data without the country and smoking variables. You do not need to replace the original data.

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Object assignment

to define a new variable:


nhanes$new_variable<-1

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
transform()

equivalently, use the transform() function:


minidata <- transform(minidata, new_variable = 1)


here, transform() returns a version of minidata with a new variable added called new_variable
= 1 defines the values of new_variable
what would happen if I didn’t include include minidata <-?

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
transform()

minidata <- transform(minidata, new_variable = 1)


in general, the second argument is: variable name = definition of new variable

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
transform() with piping

with piping:


minidata <- minidata |>
  transform(new_variable = 1)


minidata now looks like this:


minidata |> head()
#|   bmxht new_variable
#| 1 179.5            1
#| 2 174.2            1
#| 3 152.9            1
#| 4    NA            1
#| 5    NA            1
#| 6 173.3            1

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
transform() with piping

to convert bmxht to inches:


minidata <- minidata |>
  transform(height = bmxht * 0.3937008)


minidata now looks like this:


minidata |> head()
#|   bmxht new_variable   height
#| 1 179.5            1 70.66929
#| 2 174.2            1 68.58268
#| 3 152.9            1 60.19685
#| 4    NA            1       NA
#| 5    NA            1       NA
#| 6 173.3            1 68.22835

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Defining missing values

the replace() strategy for defining missing values, from Session 6 of A Slower Introduction to R can be combined with transform() and piping:


nhanes <- nhanes |>
  transform(ltpa_vigorous = replace(pad820, 
                                    pad820 == 7777 | pad820 == 9999,
                                    NA))

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Defining missing values

ltpa_vigorous looks like this:


nhanes$ltpa_vigorous |> summary()
#|    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#|    1.00   30.00   45.00   60.44   60.00  900.00    4480


whereas pad820 looks like this:


nhanes$pad820 |> summary()
#|    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#|    1.00   30.00   45.00   97.57   60.00 9999.00    4466

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Defining categorical variables

all of the strategies from Session 7 of A Slower Introduction to R can be combined with transform() and piping

title: Session 1: Piping
Session 1: Piping
text:
Labeling categorical variables

country looks like this:


nhanes$country |> table(useNA='always')
#| 
#|   USA Other  <NA> 
#|  6519  1617    17


whereas dmdborn4 looks like this:


nhanes$dmdborn4 |> table(useNA='always')
#| 
#|    1    2 <NA> 
#| 6519 1617   17

title: Session 1: Piping
Session 1: Piping
text:
Categorizing continuous variables

or, using base_when() from my baseverse package:


nhanes <- nhanes |>
  transform(cholesterol = base_when(
    'Desirable' = (lbxtc < 200),
    'Borderline high' = (lbxtc >= 200) & (lbxtc < 240),
    'High' = (lbxtc >= 240)
  ))

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Categorizing continuous variables

cholesterol looks like this:


nhanes$cholesterol |> table(useNA='always')
#| 
#|       Desirable Borderline high            High            <NA> 
#|            3695            1397             625            2436


whereas lbxtc looks like this:


nhanes$lbxtc |> summary()
#|    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#|      62     157     184     187     213     438    2436

title: Session 1: Piping
text:
Exercise 5

Use piping and transform() to define a new variable for weight (bmxwt) in pounds. Hint: bmxwt is in kilograms and there are 2.204623 pounds in 1 kilgoram.
Use piping, transform(), and factor() to define a new variable called sex. This should be a labelled version of the original gender variable (riagendr). Values of 1 are used for males and values of 0 are used for females. Not:, this should end up matching the existing gender variable.
